name: Tuskegee University
formerNames: Tuskegee Normal School for Colored Teachers
description: Chartered in 1881 after an agreement between Black community leader Lewis Adams and former Confederate colonel Wilbur F. Foster, with Booker T. Washington as first principal. Tuskegee became the flagship of Washington's self-help and industrial-education philosophy, home to George Washington Carver's research and the training ground of the Tuskegee Airmen. Its economic legacy runs from Washington's National Negro Business League to alumni such as builder Herman J. Russell, broadcaster Tom Joyner and inventor-entrepreneur Lonnie Johnson.

facts.d: Lewis Adams secured state funding for a Black normal school in exchange for delivering Black votes to Wilbur F. Foster; Booker T. Washington opened the school on July 4, 1881.
Washington founded the National Negro Business League in 1900; Tuskegee alumni such as Jake Simmons Jr. later presided over it.
Tuskegee trained the Tuskegee Airmen in WWII and today describes itself as a leading producer of Black aerospace engineers (self-reported).

connections.label: Booker T. Washington founded the NNBL, 1900

name: Alabama A&M University
formerNames: Huntsville State Normal School for Negroes
State Normal and Industrial School of Huntsville
The State Agricultural and Mechanical College for Negroes
State Agricultural and Mechanical Institute for Negroes
description: Founded in 1875 by formerly enslaved educator William Hooper Councill as a normal school in Huntsville, it became Alabama's 1890 land-grant institution. Sitting next to NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center and Redstone Arsenal, AAMU feeds Huntsville's aerospace and defense-contracting economy — alumni include Hall of Famer-turned-contractor John Stallworth (Madison Research Corp.) and EyeMail founder Lisa S. Jones.

facts.d: William Hooper Councill, the first president, opened the school in 1875 as Huntsville State Normal School for Negroes.
It became the State Agricultural and Mechanical College for Negroes in 1896 and took its present name in 1969.
Alumni work across Huntsville's NASA and defense-contracting cluster; Stallworth's MRC and Cynthia Crutchfield's career both grew from it.

name: Alabama State University
affiliation: Thurgood Marshall College Fund; American Missionary Association (early support)
description: Begun in 1867 as the Lincoln Normal School in Marion by nine formerly enslaved men, it moved to Montgomery in 1887 under president William Burns Paterson. ASU students, faculty and alumni were central to the Montgomery Bus Boycott — Ralph Abernathy, Fred Gray and Jo Ann Robinson's network — and the school still anchors Montgomery's Black professional class.

facts.d: The Lincoln Normal School of Marion (1867) relocated to Montgomery in 1887 and became Alabama State University in 1969.
Alumni include Ralph Abernathy, attorney Fred Gray and Fred Shuttlesworth; ASU faculty helped print boycott leaflets in 1955.
ASU's Mobile extension center (1927) became today's Bishop State Community College.

connections.label: AMA supported the early Lincoln Normal School

name: Miles College
description: Founded in 1898 by the Colored (now Christian) Methodist Episcopal Church just west of Birmingham, Miles was a staging ground for the Birmingham civil-rights movement and the 1962 Selective Buying Campaign — a student-led economic boycott of downtown merchants. Alumni include Birmingham's first Black mayor Richard Arrington Jr., Alabama's first Black federal judge U. W. Clemon, and insurance executive-congressman Bennett M. Stewart.

facts.d: Organized by the CME Church; named Miles Memorial College until 1941.
Miles students launched the 1962 boycott of Birmingham stores that refused to hire Black clerks — an early use of consumer economic power.
Produced Birmingham mayor Richard Arrington Jr. and judge U. W. Clemon.

name: Oakwood University
description: Opened in 1896 by the General Conference of Seventh-day Adventists on a former plantation in Huntsville, Oakwood is the only HBCU owned and operated by the Adventist church. It is known for its music (the Aeolians choir, Take 6) and ministry training; alumni include insurance entrepreneur and civil-rights leader T. R. M. Howard and Senate Chaplain Barry Black.

facts.d: Sponsored by the General Conference until 2014, then by the North American Division.
Touring choir founded in 1946 by Dr. Eva B. Dykes; has performed at the White House and Kennedy Center.
Joined the United Negro College Fund in 1964.

connections.label: founded by the SDA General Conference

name: Stillman College
description: Authorized by the (Southern) Presbyterian General Assembly in 1875 and opened in 1876 on the idea of pastor Charles Allen Stillman to train Black ministers, it became a four-year college in 1948. Alumni include Marine Lt. Gen. Willie J. Williams, legislator Michael Figures and Olympic long-jump champion Jeff Henderson.

facts.d: Conceived 'for the training of colored men for the ministry' by Charles A. Stillman of First Presbyterian, Tuscaloosa.
Tuscaloosa Institute (1876–1895), Stillman Institute (1895–1948), Stillman College (1948–).

name: Talladega College
affiliation: American Missionary Association; United Church of Christ; UNCF
description: Alabama's oldest private historically Black liberal-arts college, begun in 1867 by formerly enslaved men William Savery and Thomas Tarrant with American Missionary Association and Freedmen's Bureau support. Talladega produced a striking roster of business pioneers — ad-agency founder Barbara Gardner Proctor, millionaire dermatologist-banker Theodore K. Lawless, Walker Company manager Willard Ransom and Pepsi bottler William R. Harvey.

facts.d: Savery and Tarrant met at a Freedmen's Bureau convention in Mobile in 1866; the AMA bought the building and the Bureau the land.
Hale Woodruff's murals in Savery Library anchor the William R. Harvey Museum of Art (opened 2020).
Alumni founded or led Proctor & Gardner Advertising, Service Federal Savings and Loan and the Madam C. J. Walker Manufacturing Co.

name: Selma University
formerNames: Alabama Baptist Normal and Theological School
description: Founded in 1878 by Alabama's Black Baptist convention to train ministers and teachers, it took the Selma University name in 1908. Its graduates include civil-rights leader Fred Shuttlesworth, Juanita Abernathy and federal-workers union president Everett Kelley.

facts.d: The Black Baptist convention voted in 1877 to locate the school in Selma; William H. McAlpine was among the founders.
Became Selma University on May 14, 1908.

connections.label: founded by Alabama's Black Baptist convention

name: Bishop State Community College
formerNames: S. D. Bishop State Junior College
description: Begun in 1927 as the Mobile extension of Alabama State College and made a junior college in 1936, Bishop State absorbed Southwest State Technical College and Carver State Technical College in 1991. It is Mobile's public HBCU for workforce and transfer education.

facts.d: Started as Alabama State's Mobile center; named for first president S. D. Bishop in 1971.
Southwest State Technical (est. 1947) and Carver State Technical (est. 1962) were consolidated into it in 1991.

name: Gadsden State Community College
description: Formed in 1985 by merging several Gadsden-area colleges, it carries HBCU designation through the Gadsden Vocational Trade School, opened in 1960 for Black students and later renamed Gadsden State Technical Institute — today its Valley Street Campus. The school was designated a historically Black college in 1997.

facts.d: The Valley Street Campus descends from the 1960 Gadsden Vocational Trade School for Black students; designated HBCU in 1997.
Combines the Alabama School of Trades (1925), Gadsden State Junior College (1965) and Ayers State Technical College (2003).

name: H. Councill Trenholm State Community College
formerNames: H. Councill Trenholm State Technical College
description: A public historically Black technical and community college in Montgomery named for Alabama State president H. Councill Trenholm. Its 2001 consolidation with John M. Patterson Technical College kept the Trenholm name to preserve Title III-B HBCU funding.

facts.d: The consolidated name kept Title III-B eligibility that the historically Black college held before the merger.
Renamed from State Technical College to Community College.

sources.label: Wikipedia — H. Councill Trenholm State Community College

name: J. F. Drake State Community and Technical College
formerNames: J. F. Drake State Technical College
description: Opened in 1961 in Huntsville as a vocational-technical school for Black students and named for Alabama A&M president Joseph Fanning Drake, Drake State trains technicians for Huntsville's aerospace, manufacturing and defense economy.

facts.d: Honors Joseph Fanning Drake, longtime president of Alabama A&M.
Feeds technicians into the Huntsville aerospace/defense cluster.

sources.label: Wikipedia — J. F. Drake State Technical College
Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Lawson State Community College
formerNames: Theodore Alfred Lawson State Junior College
description: Started in 1949 as Wenonah State Technical Institute; joined with Wenonah State Junior College in 1973 and was named for first president Theodore Alfred Lawson. It absorbed Bessemer State Technical College in 2005.

facts.d: Technical and junior-college divisions merged in 1973 as T. A. Lawson State.
Bessemer State Technical College became its Bessemer Campus in 2005.

name: Shelton State Community College
description: Tuscaloosa's community college, established under its current name in 1979, gained its historically Black designation through the 1994 merger with C. A. Fredd State Technical College, the city's Black technical college; the Fredd campus continues as part of Shelton State.

facts.d: C. A. Fredd State Technical College merged into Shelton State in 1994.
Formed when Shelton State combined with the Tuscaloosa branch of Brewer State.

name: C. A. Fredd State Technical College
fate: Merged into Shelton State Community College in 1994, which now operates the Fredd campus.
description: Created by the Alabama legislature in 1963 as the Tuscaloosa State Trade School for Black students, renamed Tuscaloosa State Technical College in 1974 and C. A. Fredd State Technical College in 1976. Its 1994 merger gave Shelton State its HBCU status.

facts.d: Trade school (1963), Tuscaloosa State Technical College (1974), C. A. Fredd State Technical College (1976).
Became part of Shelton State Community College.

name: Concordia College Alabama
fate: Closed after the spring 2018 semester, citing years of financial distress and declining enrollment.
description: Opened in 1922 in a rented cottage after Black Lutheran congregations in Alabama's Black Belt — built largely through educator Rosa J. Young — petitioned the Missouri Synod. It was the only historically Black member of the Concordia University System and closed in 2018.

facts.d: The sole HBCU in the LCMS's Concordia University System.
Educator Rosa J. Young, who taught there, is credited with building the Black Lutheran congregations behind it.

name: Daniel Payne College
fate: A 1977 tornado badly damaged the campus; with mounting debts it filed for bankruptcy in 1978 and closed in 1979.
description: Founded in Selma in 1889 by the AME Church and named for Bishop Daniel Payne — the first Black college president in the U.S. — it moved to Birmingham in 1922. Airport and interstate expansion forced relocations, and a tornado in 1977 led to its closure.

facts.d: Bishop Daniel Payne was the AME's sixth bishop and led Wilberforce University.
Relocated to Woodlawn in Birmingham in 1922; moved again in 1974.

name: Jackson State University
affiliation: Thurgood Marshall College Fund; American Baptist Home Mission Society (founder)
description: Founded in Natchez in 1877 by the American Baptist Home Mission Society, it moved to Jackson in 1882 and became a state school in 1940. JSU is Mississippi's largest HBCU and its urban research university; alumni include Walter Payton, Secretary of Education Rod Paige, Rep. Bennie Thompson and Jackson Advocate founder Percy Greene.

facts.d: Opened as Natchez Seminary (1877) under the American Baptist Home Mission Society.
Police killed two people at Alexander Hall in May 1970, days after Kent State.
Walter Payton parlayed his career into heavy-equipment, racing and restaurant ventures.

name: Alcorn State University
description: Founded in 1871 on the former Oakland College campus with Senator Hiram Revels as first president, Alcorn was the first Black land-grant college in the United States. Its alumni include insurance and banking pioneer Joseph Edison Walker (Universal Life, Tri-State Bank), Medgar and Charles Evers, Alex Haley and Steve McNair.

facts.d: Land-grant from its founding in 1871.
The first Black U.S. senator was Alcorn's founding president.
Alumnus J. E. Walker co-founded Memphis's Universal Life Insurance (1923) and Tri-State Bank (1946).

name: Mississippi Valley State University
description: Created by the legislature in 1946 and opened in 1950 in the Delta as Mississippi Vocational College — partly to keep Black students out of white state schools — MVSU became a university in 1974. It is best known for Jerry Rice and the record-setting 1984 Delta Devils offense.

facts.d: Legislation signed April 5, 1946; opened 1950.
The Hall of Fame receiver played at Valley 1981–84.

name: Rust College
description: Founded in 1866 by Northern missionaries of the Methodist Episcopal Church's Freedmen's Aid Society, Rust is Mississippi's oldest private HBCU. Its early alumni include journalist Ida B. Wells and Mound Bayou banker Charles Banks; later graduates include Las Vegas pain-medicine entrepreneur Godwin Maduka and Hi Records chief Willie Mitchell.

facts.d: Shaw University (1870) became Rust University in 1892 to avoid confusion with Shaw University in Raleigh; Rust College from 1915.
Charles Banks (Bank of Mound Bayou) and Ida B. Wells (Free Speech) attended.
Bought the closed Mississippi Industrial College campus across the street in 2008.

connections.label: founded by the Freedmen's Aid Society

name: Tougaloo College
affiliation: American Missionary Association; United Church of Christ; Disciples of Christ; UNCF
description: Established in 1869 by the American Missionary Association on a former plantation north of Jackson, Tougaloo was the 'cradle' of Mississippi's civil-rights movement, hosting the 1963 Woolworth sit-in organizers. Alumni include Justice Reuben V. Anderson, Rep. Bennie Thompson, author Anne Moody and Jackson Medical Mall founder Aaron Shirley.

facts.d: The AMA bought the plantation land to educate freedpeople.
The Disciples of Christ's Southern Christian Institute merged into Tougaloo in 1954.
Tougaloo students led the 1963 Jackson Woolworth's sit-in.

name: Coahoma Community College
formerNames: Coahoma Junior College and Agricultural High School
description: Grew out of the Coahoma County Agricultural High School (1924) and added a junior college in 1949; renamed Coahoma Community College in 1989. It serves the Mississippi Delta from a rural campus near Clarksdale.

facts.d: Began as a 1924 county agricultural high school for Black students.
Became Coahoma Community College in 1989.

name: Hinds Community College–Utica
description: Founded in 1903 as Utica Normal and Industrial Institute by Tuskegee graduate William H. Holtzclaw on the Booker T. Washington model, it became Utica Junior College and was merged into Hinds Junior College in 1982 under a federal desegregation court order. The Utica campus retains its HBCU identity.

facts.d: Founder William H. Holtzclaw was a Tuskegee graduate who replicated its industrial-education model.
Merged with Hinds in 1982 as part of a class-action racial discrimination case.

connections.label: founded by Tuskegee graduate William H. Holtzclaw

name: Mary Holmes College
affiliation: Presbyterian Church (Board of Missions for Freedmen)
fate: Lost SACS accreditation in 2002 and closed in March 2005 after failing to attract enough students and funds.
description: Opened in 1892 in Jackson as Mary Holmes Seminary — conceived by missionary Rev. Mead Holmes and his daughter Mary — under the Presbyterian Board of Missions for Freedmen, later relocating to West Point. It became a junior college in 1959 and closed in 2005.

facts.d: Named for Mary Emilie Holmes, who with her father Mead Holmes conceived the school.
Lost accreditation in 2002; closed 2005.

connections.label: funded and overseen by the Board

name: Mississippi Industrial College
fate: Enrollment fell after Mississippi's community colleges desegregated; the campus closed in 1982 and was bought by Rust College in 2008.
description: Founded in 1905 by the Mississippi Conference of the Colored Methodist Episcopal Church under Bishop Elias Cottrell, MIC educated generations of north Mississippi teachers and CME clergy. Its campus is on the National Register of Historic Places.

facts.d: Bishop Elias Cottrell, born enslaved, led its founding.
Listed on the National Register in 1980; acquired by Rust College in 2008.

connections.label: founded by the CME Mississippi Conference

name: Natchez College
affiliation: Mississippi Black Baptist State Missionary Convention
fate: Stopped granting bachelor's degrees in the 1960s and, as Natchez Junior College, closed in 1989 (some lists give 1993).
description: Founded in 1884 by the Baptist State Missionary Convention under George W. Gayles, Natchez College trained Black teachers and ministers in southwest Mississippi; Booker T. Washington visited in 1908. Alumni include Mound Bayou banker Eugene P. Booze and author Anne Moody.

facts.d: Founded through the Baptist State Missionary Convention led by George W. Gayles.
Alumnus Eugene P. Booze co-founded the Bank of Mound Bayou (1904).

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

connections.label: founded by Mississippi's Black Baptist convention

name: J. P. Campbell College
fate: Seized by the state through eminent domain and closed in 1964; scholars link the decision to its role in the Jackson civil-rights movement.
description: Founded in Vicksburg in 1890 by the AME Church and moved to Jackson in 1898, Campbell College admitted students expelled from other schools for civil-rights activism before the state took its land in 1964.

facts.d: Admitted students expelled for civil-rights activism.
The state acquired the campus in 1964.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Okolona College
affiliation: American Church Institute for Negroes (Episcopal), from 1921
fate: Closed in 1965 amid financial difficulties (about 60% of its budget came from donations) as public options opened after the Civil Rights Act of 1964.
description: Founded in 1902 by Wallace A. Battle on the Tuskegee industrial model, Okolona joined the Episcopal Church's American Church Institute for Negroes in 1921 and was reorganized in 1933 into a high school and two-year junior college.

facts.d: Battle, influenced by Booker T. Washington, taught agriculture, mechanical arts and teacher training.
Teacher Ulysses S. Baskin was murdered on commencement day amid racist harassment.

connections.label: American Church Institute for Negroes affiliate from 1921

name: Prentiss Institute
fate: Phased out lower grades after 1959 and closed in 1989; the campus is now a museum and historic district.
description: Founded in 1907 by Jonas Edward and Bertha LaBranche Johnson in a former plantation house, Prentiss combined academic and industrial training, became a junior college in 1931 and enrolled about 700 students by 1957.

facts.d: The Johnsons lived in the plantation house where classes began.
Received Rosenwald funding and ran a Heifer International dairy program.

name: Saints Junior College
fate: The junior college faded after president Arenia Mallory's death in 1977; the academy closed in 2006 as the Delta's population declined.
description: Founded in 1918 by COGIC founder Charles H. Mason as the Saints Industrial and Literary School, it grew under Arenia Mallory (1926–1977) into a respected academy and junior college in Holmes County.

facts.d: A ministry of St. Paul's Church of God in Christ, Lexington.
Mallory (a Jackson State alumna) led it for 51 years.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Mount Hermon Female Seminary
fate: The AMA closed it in 1924 because it already operated Tougaloo College nearby.
description: Founded in 1875 by Sarah Ann Dickey on the Mount Holyoke model to educate Black women, it was supported by the Slater Fund and taken over by the American Missionary Association after Dickey's death in 1903.

facts.d: Dickey patterned it on her alma mater.
The AMA consolidated its Mississippi work at Tougaloo.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

name: Southern Christian Institute
fate: Merged into Tougaloo College in 1954; its Edwards campus, renamed Mt. Beulah, later hosted civil-rights organizations.
description: Founded in 1882 by the Disciples of Christ to educate African Americans, SCI merged with Tougaloo in 1954 — the source of Tougaloo's Disciples of Christ affiliation.

facts.d: Founded by the Christian Church (Disciples of Christ).
Joined Tougaloo College.

sources.label: Wikipedia — List of historically black colleges and universities

connections.label: founded by the Disciples of Christ

name: Tom Joyner
wealthNote: Estimate: founder-owner of Reach Media and decades as a top-paid syndicated host; no audited figure published.
hbcuStory: Born in Tuskegee and graduated from Tuskegee Institute with a sociology degree; he began broadcasting in Montgomery right after college.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Tuskegee, Alabama, he worked small-market radio jobs in Montgomery, Memphis and St. Louis before reaching major markets.
breakthrough: Famous as 'the Fly Jock' for commuting daily between Dallas (KKDA) and Chicago (WGCI) from 1985 to 1993, he signed with ABC Radio in 1994 to syndicate The Tom Joyner Morning Show nationally and founded Reach Media to own and monetize it.
legacy: His Tom Joyner Foundation has raised more than $65 million for HBCU students since 1998; Reach Media built a Black-audience syndication business later folded into Urban One.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built his own company to own the morning show, events and digital properties rather than remaining talent-for-hire.
ABC Radio deal took the show to millions of listeners until his retirement on December 13, 2019.
Reach Media came under Radio One (now Urban One) ownership in the 2000s.

legacyDetail.d: The Tom Joyner Foundation has raised more than $65 million since 1998.
Used 'HBCU of the Month' on-air features to channel listener money to Black colleges.

name: Herman J. Russell
wealthNote: Estimate: personal net worth never published; based on ownership of the largest minority-owned construction/real-estate firm.
hbcuStory: Earned a building-construction degree from Tuskegee Institute (1953), applying Booker T. Washington's trades-to-ownership model; he also attended Clark College.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in Atlanta's Summerhill neighborhood learning plastering from his father, Rogers Russell, and bought his first lot as a teenager.
breakthrough: Founded H.J. Russell & Associates in 1953 (incorporated 1957); it plastered Atlanta-Fulton County Stadium (1963), built Citizens Trust Bank's headquarters (1969) and worked on Coca-Cola's headquarters, the 1996 Olympic stadium and Hartsfield-Jackson airport.
legacy: Grew H.J. Russell & Company into the largest minority-owned real-estate and construction firm in the U.S., became the first Black member and later president of the Atlanta Chamber of Commerce, and handed the companies to his children Michael, Jerome and Donata in 2003.

breakthroughDetail.d: H.J. Russell & Company became the largest minority-owned real estate and construction company in the U.S.
Colony Square (with Holder), Coca-Cola HQ, Olympic stadium and airport work.
His companies included Concessions International, an airport food-service operator.

legacyDetail.d: Son Michael Russell became CEO of H.J. Russell & Company after his 2003 retirement.
A confidant of Martin Luther King Jr.; Horatio Alger Award 1991.

sources.label: New Georgia Encyclopedia — Herman J. Russell

name: Claude A. Barnett
hbcuStory: Attended Tuskegee Institute 1904–1906, graduating in 1906; he later served as a Tuskegee trustee from 1932 to 1965.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Sanford, Florida, he worked as a postal clerk in Chicago after Tuskegee and ran a mail-order photo and cosmetics business on the side.
breakthrough: Founded the Associated Negro Press in 1919, a wire service that supplied news to scores of Black newspapers for nearly fifty years.
legacy: The ANP made Black-press syndication a business; Barnett also advised the USDA on Black farmers and married actress-singer Etta Moten.

breakthroughDetail.d: Supplied stories to Black newspapers nationwide through the 1960s.
Ran a mail-order cosmetics firm after leaving the Post Office.

legacyDetail.d: On the Tuskegee board 1932–1965.

sources.label: BlackAmericaWeb — Little Known Black History Fact: Claude A. Barnett

name: Jake Simmons Jr.
hbcuStory: Booker T. Washington, a guest at the Simmons ranch, persuaded him to enroll at Tuskegee Institute, where he graduated in 1919.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Indian Territory (later Haskell, Oklahoma) to a Creek freedman ranching family.
breakthrough: Became an oil broker dealing with Skelly Oil and Phillips Petroleum, built the Simmons Royalty Co., and brokered partnerships with Phillips and Signal Oil and Gas to open oil fields in Liberia, Nigeria and Ghana.
legacy: Called the most successful Black entrepreneur in petroleum history; in 1969 he became the first Black member of the National Petroleum Council and presided over the National Negro Business League.

breakthroughDetail.d: His own oil-lease and royalty brokerage.
Partnered with Phillips Petroleum and Signal Oil and Gas in West Africa.
First Black person appointed.

legacyDetail.d: Led Washington's National Negro Business League; also Oklahoma NAACP president.

sources.label: Oklahoma Historical Society — Simmons, Jake, Jr.

name: Vertner Woodson Tandy
hbcuStory: Studied architectural drawing at Tuskegee Institute in 1904 before transferring to Cornell (B.Arch. 1907).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Lexington, Kentucky, to building contractor Henry A. Tandy.
breakthrough: Co-founded Tandy & Foster in New York and became the first Black registered architect in New York State; designed St. Philip's Episcopal Church in Harlem and Villa Lewaro, Madam C. J. Walker's Irvington estate.
legacy: One of the seven founders ('Jewels') of Alpha Phi Alpha; his Harlem buildings, including the Ivey Delph Apartments, are landmarks of Black professional enterprise.

breakthroughDetail.d: Black-owned architecture firm co-founded with George Washington Foster.
Designed the mansion for Madam C. J. Walker, the era's richest Black businesswoman.

legacyDetail.d: One of seven founders at Cornell in 1906; designed the fraternity pin.

connections.label: designed Villa Lewaro for Madam C. J. Walker, 1918

name: Ray Nagin
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in accounting from Tuskegee University in 1978.
humbleBeginnings: Born at New Orleans' Charity Hospital and raised in the city's 7th Ward.
breakthrough: Joined Cox Communications' New Orleans system as controller in 1985 and by 1989 was vice president and general manager of Cox Louisiana; he also co-owned the New Orleans Brass hockey team before winning the mayoralty in 2002.
legacy: Led New Orleans through Hurricane Katrina (2002–2010) but was convicted in 2014 on 20 federal corruption counts and sentenced to ten years — a cautionary arc from executive to public office.

breakthroughDetail.d: VP and general manager of Cox Communications' Louisiana operations by 1989.
Ran as an outsider executive and served two terms as mayor (2002–2010).

legacyDetail.d: Convicted February 2014 of bribery, wire fraud and money laundering.

name: Bill Winston
hbcuStory: Graduated from Tuskegee Institute in 1967, then flew fighters in Vietnam (Distinguished Flying Cross).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Tuskegee, Alabama; served six years in the Air Force before joining IBM as a marketer in 1973.
breakthrough: Rose to IBM regional marketing manager, left in 1985 for ministry, and founded Living Word Christian Center (1988–90), which bought the 33-acre Forest Park Mall in Illinois.
legacy: Built a church-anchored business ecosystem — the Joseph Business School, Forest Park Plaza, bookstores, an aviation company and Washington Plaza in Tuskegee.

breakthroughDetail.d: Living Word acquired the 33-acre Forest Park Mall; first service there New Year's Eve 1997.
Founded an accredited campus and online business school in Forest Park.

legacyDetail.d: Lists Washington Plaza in Tuskegee among his ventures.

name: Keenen Ivory Wayans
hbcuStory: Attended Tuskegee on an engineering scholarship and joined Alpha Phi Alpha; he left one semester before graduating to pursue comedy.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Harlem, one of ten children, raised in the Fulton Houses projects.
breakthrough: Created, wrote and starred in In Living Color for Fox (1990–94), launching the careers of Jim Carrey, Jennifer Lopez and his siblings.
legacy: Turned the Wayans family into a film franchise (Scary Movie, White Chicks) and set a model for Black creator-owned comedy.

breakthroughDetail.d: Fox sketch show he created and ran, 1990–94.
Directed Scary Movie (2000), among the top-grossing films by a Black director at the time.

legacyDetail.d: Launched multiple careers from his show.

sources.label: Television Academy — Keenen Ivory Wayans interview

name: Lionel Richie
wealthNote: Estimate from 90M+ records sold and catalog ownership; no audited figure published.
hbcuStory: Attended Tuskegee Institute on a tennis scholarship and earned a B.S. in economics (accounting minor); he formed R&B groups on campus that led into the Commodores.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up on the Tuskegee Institute campus, where his grandmother taught and his family lived.
breakthrough: Joined the Commodores in 1968, who signed with Motown; his solo album Can't Slow Down (1983) sold over 20 million copies and he co-wrote 'We Are the World' (1985).
legacy: Over 90 million records sold; owns a lucrative songwriting catalog and became the Prince's Trust's first Global Ambassador.

breakthroughDetail.d: Moved from Tuskegee campus bands to Motown stardom.
Over 20 million copies worldwide.

legacyDetail.d: Songwriting royalties are the core asset.

connections.label: B.S. Economics (1974 per Tuskegee alumni list)

name: Lonnie Johnson
wealthNote: Estimate from royalty income and the 2013 ~$73M arbitration award.
hbcuStory: Earned a B.S. in mechanical engineering (1973) and an M.S. in nuclear engineering (1975) at Tuskegee; Tuskegee gave him an honorary doctorate in 2018.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Mobile, Alabama, he built a robot ('Linex') as a teen and won a state science fair.
breakthrough: While an Air Force and NASA JPL engineer he invented the Super Soaker, licensed to Larami (bought by Hasbro in 1995); it sold about $200 million in 1991 alone, and he founded Johnson Research and Development in 1991.
legacy: Won a nearly $73 million arbitration award against Hasbro in 2013 over royalties, and reinvested in Atlanta energy-tech ventures (Excellatron, JEMS) on Sweet Auburn.

breakthroughDetail.d: ~$200M in sales in 1991; cumulative sales approached $1B by 2013.
Awarded nearly $73M in unpaid royalties from Hasbro in 2013.
National Inventors Hall of Fame, 2022.

legacyDetail.d: Excellatron Solid State and Johnson Electro-Mechanical Systems pursue batteries and the JTEC heat engine.

sources.label: National Inventors Hall of Fame — Lonnie Johnson
BBC — The father of the Super Soaker

name: Kelly Alexander Sr.
hbcuStory: Attended Tuskegee Institute (B.A.) and later the Renouard College of Embalming.
humbleBeginnings: Son of Zechariah Alexander, owner of Charlotte's only Black funeral home.
breakthrough: Ran the family's Alexander Funeral Home while rebuilding the North Carolina NAACP, which he led from 1948 to 1984.
legacy: Known as 'Mr. NAACP,' he chaired the national NAACP board in 1983–84; the funeral business funded a family political dynasty.

breakthroughDetail.d: Expanded the state conference dramatically.

legacyDetail.d: The funeral home gave economic independence for activism.

sources.label: New York Times — Kelly Alexander of N.A.A.C.P. Dies

name: Daniel James Jr.
hbcuStory: Attended Tuskegee Institute (1937–42) and learned to fly in its Civilian Pilot Training Program, then instructed Tuskegee Airmen.
humbleBeginnings: Youngest of 17 children; his mother ran a private school in Pensacola.
breakthrough: Flew combat missions in Korea and Vietnam and in 1975 became the first African American four-star general.
legacy: Commanded NORAD; a symbol of the Tuskegee aviation legacy.

breakthroughDetail.d: Promoted 1975.

legacyDetail.d: Product of Tuskegee's flight program.

name: Ralph Ellison
hbcuStory: Studied music at Tuskegee Institute (1933–36) on scholarship, leaving before graduation for New York.
humbleBeginnings: Raised in Oklahoma City by a widowed mother who cleaned houses.

breakthrough: Became co-owner and editor of the Memphis Free Speech and Headlight and launched her anti-lynching campaign.
legacy: Co-founded the NAACP; Pulitzer special citation (2020).

legacyDetail.d: 2020, posthumous.

name: Godwin Maduka
hbcuStory: Graduated summa cum laude from Rust College in 1984 with a chemistry degree.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Nkerehi (now Umuchukwu), Anambra State, Nigeria.
breakthrough: After pharmacy (Mercer), medicine (Tennessee) and Harvard/Beth Israel anesthesiology training, he founded the Las Vegas Pain Institute and Medical Center in 1999, expanding to six more Southern Nevada locations.
legacy: Reinvested in his hometown — leading its renaming to Umuchukwu and building medical facilities — and ran for governor of Anambra.

breakthroughDetail.d: Grew to seven locations.
Chemistry, pharmacy, M.D. and anesthesiology training.

name: Willie Mitchell
hbcuStory: Attended Rust College.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Ashland, Mississippi; led bands in Memphis clubs.
breakthrough: Joined Hi Records in 1961 as artist and producer and took over the label in 1970, producing Al Green's string of 1970s hits at Royal Studios.
legacy: Royal Studios remained a Memphis landmark run by his family.

breakthroughDetail.d: Built the Memphis soul sound.
Reunited for I Can't Stop (2003).

legacyDetail.d: Family-run studio legacy.

name: Aaron Shirley
hbcuStory: Graduated from Tougaloo College in 1955 before Meharry Medical College.
humbleBeginnings: Grew up in rural Mississippi.
breakthrough: Became the first Black pediatric resident at the University of Mississippi Medical Center and pioneered community health centers.
legacy: Founded the Jackson Medical Mall, converting a dying shopping mall into a health and business hub; MacArthur Fellow.

breakthroughDetail.d: Redeveloped a failing mall into a medical campus.

legacyDetail.d: Recognized for community health work.

name: Lemuel L. Foster
hbcuStory: Attended Tougaloo College.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Meridian, Mississippi; led the Atlanta Urban League from 1920.
breakthrough: Worked for Victory Life Insurance in New York in the 1920s, then served as an executive in R. H. Macy & Company's personnel division (1945–49) — an early Black executive at a major department store.
legacy: Continued as a race-relations consultant and Harlem community leader.

name: Reuben V. Anderson
hbcuStory: Graduated from Tougaloo College in 1965, then became one of the first Black graduates of the University of Mississippi law school (1967).
humbleBeginnings: Born in Jackson, Mississippi.
breakthrough: Became the first Black justice on the Mississippi Supreme Court (1985–90), after civil-rights practice and NAACP LDF work.
legacy: Later a partner at Phelps Dunbar; chaired Mississippi's 2020 flag commission.

breakthroughDetail.t: First Black Mississippi Supreme Court justice.

name: Anne Moody
hbcuStory: Attended Natchez Junior College on a basketball scholarship, then earned a B.S. from Tougaloo College in 1964.
humbleBeginnings: Born to sharecroppers near Centreville, Mississippi.
breakthrough: Joined the 1963 Jackson Woolworth's sit-in and wrote the memoir Coming of Age in Mississippi (1968).
legacy: Her memoir remains a core civil-rights text.

breakthroughDetail.d: Jackson, 1963.

legacyDetail.d: Published 1968.

name: Eugene P. Booze
hbcuStory: Attended Natchez College, then apprenticed in merchandising and cotton trading.
humbleBeginnings: Born in Adams County, Mississippi.
breakthrough: Co-founded the Bank of Mound Bayou with brother-in-law Charles Banks in 1904 and the Farmer's Cooperative Mercantile Company (1909–22); he owned extensive cotton land.
legacy: Married Mary Montgomery, daughter of Mound Bayou founder Isaiah Montgomery, joining the town's leading business family; he was ambushed and killed in 1939.

Co-founded 1909.

legacyDetail.d: Son-in-law of Isaiah Montgomery.
